asDecan.p: Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Scorpio. Every sign is cut into three decans of ten degrees, each with its own planet and its own small card, and in the Golden Dawn order this opening slice goes to Mars. Mars also rules Scorpio, so the planet running your ten degrees is the one running the whole sign, and it works here at full strength. Scorpio is fixed water. A feeling in this sign doesn't drain away, it stays put, and Mars gives it a push. The Sun rules the next decan, with the Six of Cups, softer and a bit nostalgic, and Venus finishes the sign with the Seven, daydreams and too many options. Yours comes before the sign has mellowed at all. Death is your Sun card, the sign's own Major. Mars's own Major is The Tower, where everything comes down at once, and that's close to how a loss lands on you, even when nobody else can tell.

You feel things at full volume and mostly keep the volume to yourself. That's Mars in its own sign, a lot of force behind a feeling and a fixed sign holding it in place. A friend cancels dinner an hour before with a vague excuse, and by the time you've hung your coat back up it's been filed somewhere you'll find it again in two years. A text left on read doesn't get a second text from you. It gets a long quiet, and a decision about that person they'll never hear about. On a Sunday with nothing planned you can drift back through an old breakup, the actual conversation, word for word, and find you're angry about it all over again. At a funeral you're often the dry-eyed one in the second row. Then you get home and can't eat for a day.

The gift people don't expect is how good you are in someone else's worst week. When a friend's marriage ends or their dad dies, most people send flowers and a kind message and then hang back, because they've no idea what to say. You turn up. You'll sit at their kitchen table and let them cry without filling the gaps, and you'll ask the blunt things nobody else will, whether they're sleeping, whether they've eaten anything since Tuesday. Grief doesn't frighten you much, because you've been at the deep end of your own feelings since you were small. The same goes for bad news on paper. When the letter from the bank or the solicitor arrives, you're the one who reads every line, small print included, and then rings to ask what it actually means.

The quieter trouble is that you sometimes start grieving before anything's been lost. A relationship is going well and part of you is already rehearsing the ending. A new job is fine, genuinely fine, and you're keeping a list of exits in your head. To you it feels like being prepared. To the people around you it looks like one foot out the door. There's also the habit of making a new person pay for an old one. Someone who has never once let you down gets the guarded version of you, because somebody else did, ten years ago, and you've never quite put that down. The figure on your card is staring at three spilled cups, with two full ones standing just behind. You can be very loyal to a loss, and your partner, or the friend you made last year, usually feels it well before you do.

A redundancy, a betrayal, a death in the family, and the first thing you do is get very focused. For a few days you can look almost fine. You're the one organising, making the calls, sorting the paperwork nobody else can face. A week later it catches up with you, and it tends to come out sideways, a flash of temper at your partner over the dishes, or a late night scrolling back through every message from the person who hurt you. Mars at home won't let a feeling sit still, so it finds an outlet whether you choose one or not. The people you live with can feel shut out, and a bit wary of setting you off. What helps is physical. A long walk, a cold swim, digging out a garden bed, anything that gives Mars something to push against. Then one person you let see the mess.

What you need from a partner, underneath the intensity, is proof that they've seen you at your worst and stayed. Compliments don't do much for you. What lands is someone who doesn't flinch when you finally tell them about the bad year, or who sits with you on the anniversary of a loss without trying to cheer you up. You tell those things late, sometimes a year or more in, and how they take it is often when you decide about them. You also remember everything. The thing they said in an argument the summer before last is still in there, and you can bring it out with surprising accuracy. Partners learn that a small apology straight away works far better with you than a big one a week later. And if you're the one who's hurt, say so within the day, before it sets into one of your silences.

You're good at work other people find too heavy to hold. I see early Scorpio Suns a lot in nursing, hospice care, counselling, forensic accounting and crisis lines, jobs where something has gone wrong and someone has to look straight at it. Mars gives you the stamina for the grim middle part, the night shift, the third week of a crisis. You're the colleague who can tell a project is dead a month before anyone admits it, and who'll say so in the meeting, which doesn't always make you popular. It gets harder when a work loss turns personal. A rejected pitch or a restructure can sit with you for months, and you might stop trusting the manager who made the call long after you've moved teams. When a project goes wrong, give it a proper ending. Write down what worked and what didn't, and then close the file.

At twenty this decan often feels things so hard it's exhausting, for you and for everyone who loves you. A breakup can flatten you for most of a year, and it's easy to decide that feeling this much is just who you are and nothing can be done about it. By the mid-thirties most people with this decan have had at least one real loss and lived through it, and that changes a lot. You learn that grief does move, slowly, and you stop being so afraid of your own. You get better at turning round to count what's left. The fifties often soften the Mars side. The grudges get lighter, and a lot of early Scorpios I've seen pick up the phone around then to someone they fell out with twenty years before, and find the friendship is still mostly there.

When something upsets you, a loss, a hurt, a bad day at work, give it a set time. Twenty minutes on a timer, somewhere private. Let yourself feel all of it, cry or swear or pace the room. When the timer goes, write down a couple of things that are still standing, even small ones, the dog, a friend who texted, the fact your knee's stopped aching. Then do something with your hands for ten minutes, and washing up counts. Repeat it the next day if you need to. Most people find they need it for fewer days than they expected.
